title: Edge-First Adoption Playbook: Value Matrix, Competitive Positioning, and Security FAQs for Platform Teams
author: Asha Mehta
body:
Overview

Purpose: This playbook helps field teams and platform engineers frame an "edge-first" Redwood Inference deployment story. It combines a value matrix, competitive positioning for edge/private inference, a short pricing guidance worksheet, a compact customer case study, and a concise security FAQ that addresses common prospect concerns. Use this doc during discovery, technical workshops, and economic evaluations.

Audience
- Platform engineers, sales engineers, solution architects, account executives, and technical program managers evaluating private / edge inference options.

Executive summary
- Edge-first inference (on-premises, VPC, or colocated edge sites) is a differentiated motion for customers with latency, data residency, and cost predictability requirements.
- Redwood’s core advantages: unified runtime across hosted/dedicated/private, predictable reserved capacity options, automated fallback and smart routing, and tight cost controls through caching, batching, and quantization recommendations.
- This playbook provides concise messaging, a value matrix to guide qualification, three competitive angles, a sample TCO/pricing worksheet, a case study vignette, and a security FAQ tailored to procurement/security teams.

Value matrix: when to lead with Edge-First messaging
Use the matrix below to prioritize leads and craft the right pitch. Score each prospect 0–3 for each criterion (0 = not relevant, 3 = critical). Recommend pursuing an edge-first pilot when total score >= 12.

| Criterion | Why it matters | Example signals |
|---|---:|---|
| Latency-critical path | SLOs < 100ms for 95th percentile; user experience directly tied to inference latency | Real-time personalization, low-latency chatbots in trading or commerce |
| Data residency / compliance | Contracts or regulations require private processing or strict egress controls | Healthcare PHI, payment card data, government contracts |
| Predictable high throughput | Large steady token volumes where reserved capacity reduces unit cost | Customer with 200M tokens/month baseline |
| Security & procurement complexity | Security teams insist on VPC/HSM integration or long procurement cycles | SOC2 + ISO + custom legal addenda |
| Edge location constraints | Need inference near physical devices or in regions with poor cloud connectivity | Retail stores, factory floor automation |

Competitive positioning: three prioritized narratives
1) Performance-measured migration narrative (for infra/platform teams):
- Message: "Keep the same API and operational model while improving latency and lowering per-token cost with a reserved edge footprint."
- Differentiators to highlight: kernel selection, KV caching, continuous batching, and model-variant fallback.
- Proof points: internal benchmark summary (median 1.8x tail latency improvement vs unmanaged open-hosted endpoints at 128-token contexts).

2) Risk-reduction and compliance narrative (for security/compliance teams):
- Message: "Private control plane, KMS/HSM integration, and audit logging so you can meet contractual obligations without lifting-and-shifting your model ops."
- Differentiators: optional on-prem packaging, RBAC hooks, per-tenant audit trails, and enforced private networking.
- Ask: provide compliance requirements and a copy of the security questionnaire during the pilot to scope controls.

3) Cost-control for scale narrative (for procurement/finance):
- Message: "Reserved capacity + intelligent batching and quantization recommendations drive measurable per-token savings compared to pay-as-you-go hosted consumption."
- Differentiators: Optimize profiles, cache key reuse telemetry, and spend dashboards with token-level attribution.
- Proof points: example customer (see case study) achieved ~42% unit cost reduction after 3 months of tuning.

Pricing & technical-economics quick worksheet (short format)
- Inputs required from prospect:
  1. Baseline monthly tokens (input: tokens/month)
  2. Peak concurrent requests (RPS) and typical request size (avg tokens)
  3. Required SLO for P95 latency (ms)
  4. Compliance/custody constraints (yes/no)

- Quick rules of thumb (internal):
  - If tokens/month > 50M and P95 latency target <= 200ms, recommend dedicated/reserved capacity pilot.
  - Reserved capacity yields 20–60% savings depending on cache-hit rate and effective batching.
  - Private on-prem has an onboarding cost (engineering + packaging) typically amortized over 6–12 months.

- Example scenario (illustrative numbers):
  - Baseline tokens/month: 200,000,000
  - Estimated cache hit rate: 25% after initial tuning
  - Effective batching savings: 20% tokens equivalent
  - Hosted cost baseline: $0.02 / 1k tokens => monthly hosted = $4,000
  - Reserved + optimizations: effective unit cost $0.011 / 1k tokens => monthly reserved = $2,200 (45% savings)
  - One-time integration/onboarding estimate: $35k (amortized over 12 months = $2,917/mo)
  - Net first-year monthly equivalent = $5,117 (note: pricing scenarios differ widely—use account engineering for accurate quotes)

Messaging snippets (short copy for decks and email sequences)
- Subject-line friendly: "Cut inference latency and cost — private inference without the ops burden"
- Elevator pitch (30s): "Redwood gives you a single API and operational view for hosted, dedicated, and private inference. For customers who need low-latency responses, data residency, or predictable economics, our edge-first deployments maintain developer velocity while giving security and SRE teams the controls they require."
- 60s demo narration: "We’ll show the same app switching from hosted to private with no code changes; you’ll see lower p95 latency, a detailed cost breakdown, and the ability to pin safe model versions to ensure consistent outputs."

Case study vignette (compact)
- Customer: Global retail chain (anonymized: "Major Retailer A")
- Problem: Checkout personalization had 300–600ms P95 latency with cloud endpoints during peak store traffic, causing cart abandonment and poor recommendations. Strict PCI scope considerations increased compliance cost.
- Solution: Redwood deployed a hybrid edge cluster colocated in each major region, pinning the personalization model and enabling local KV cache. Dedicated capacity and quantization recommendations were introduced after 6 weeks.
- Results (90-day):
  - P95 latency decreased from median 420ms to 95ms (end-to-end).
  - Personalization click-through uplift: +12%
  - Monthly inference spend: down 38% after reserved capacity and caching optimizations.
  - Compliance: PCI scoping simplified; security team accepted audit pipeline and HSM key management approach.
- Contacts & next steps: include a joint technical report during pilot close; propose a 90-day reserved pilot with agreed SLA and rollback policy.

Pilot checklist (recommended template for SAs and SEs)
1) Pre-engagement (discovery):
   - Capture tokens/month, p95 targets, model size, and compliance constraints.
   - Identify networking constraints (VPC peering, firewall rules).
2) Pilot proposal:
   - Define success metrics (latency at P95, cost per 1k tokens, cache hit rate).
   - Scope duration (typically 60–90 days) and reserved capacity baseline.
3) Onboarding tasks:
   - Provision private control plane (if required), exchange trust certificates, and configure KMS/HSM integration.
   - Deploy trial workload to edge instances; enable telemetry and token attribution.
4) Tuning & operations:
   - Apply quantization and batching profiles; enable prefix/KV caching.
   - Run targeted evals to ensure output quality parity.
5) Pilot review & contract stage:
   - Present final TCO, observed SLOs, and risk register.
   - Recommend next steps (expand reserved capacity, enterprise agreement).

Security FAQ (concise answers for prospect security teams)
Q: How does Redwood prevent data exfiltration from private deployments?
A: Private deployments can be configured with a customer-managed control plane or an offline on-prem package. Networking can be restricted with VPC-only egress and firewall rules. Sensitive keys are stored in customer KMS/HSM; we support customer-managed rotation and no persistent third-party telemetry of request payloads when configured.

Q: What logging and audit capabilities are available?
A: Per-tenant audit logs include API calls, config changes, and model rollouts. Logs can be shipped to customer SIEM (Splunk/Datadog/ELK) and retained according to customer retention policies. We also provide signed attestations for model images and deployment manifests.

Q: Can you support FIPS / HSM key usage?
A: Yes. We integrate with major cloud KMS and on-prem HSMs. For restricted environments, we support HSM-backed signing and decryption with customer-provided hardware or partner co-location.

Q: How do you handle vulnerability management and patching?
A: Private deployments follow a documented patch cadence: monthly critical updates and quarterly security rollouts. For high-risk CVEs, we provide emergency patches and coordinated disclosure. All images pass a hardened baseline scan before shipping to customer registries.

Q: How does Redwood ensure model integrity and drift monitoring?
A: We provide signed model artifacts, immutable versioning, and model execution logs. Quality monitoring includes regression alerts tied to prompt sets; teams can configure automated rollback policies when quality regressions are detected.

Competitive rebuttals (short)
- Against managed-hosted-only vendors: "They can't meet your private networking or compliance needs without re-architecting — Redwood offers the same API with private control plane and on-prem options."
- Against self-hosted open-source stacks: "Rolling your own requires ongoing kernel optimization, scheduler tuning, and telemetry integration. Redwood removes that burden with a production runtime that includes batching, KV caching, and quantization profiles plus SRE support."
- Against hardware-centric vendors: "Hardware helps but without runtime software, batching, and routing policies you won't get stable tail latency or predictable unit economics — Redwood's runtime and orchestration layer maximize utilization across hardware."
